title: Bollywood Studios Ride a Consolidation Wave as Big Money Reshapes Hindi Cinema
excerpt: From Dharma Productions to Excel Entertainment, a string of high-profile stake sales and mergers signals a new era for Bollywood as outside capital pours into the industry.
body:
• Four major deals since 2024 — Dharma, Bhansali, Sikhya, and Excel — have drawn over ₹1,800 crore in fresh capital into Bollywood studios.
  • Traditional film financing has dried up and streamer spending has cooled, pushing production houses toward equity partnerships and corporate investors.
  • Bollywood studios are also expanding southward and eyeing global distribution, aiming to de-risk revenues beyond the unpredictable Hindi belt.

A String of Blockbuster Deals

Hindi cinema's boardrooms have been busier than its box offices. In the span of roughly 18 months, four marquee stake sales have reshaped Bollywood's ownership landscape, channelling fresh capital into an industry that had been running on fumes.

The wave began in 2024 when vaccine tycoon Adar Poonawalla acquired a 50 per cent stake in Karan Johar's Dharma Productions for ₹1,000 crore, valuing the storied studio at ₹2,000 crore. In December 2025, music label Saregama India invested ₹325 crore in Sanjay Leela Bhansali's Bhansali Productions, securing exclusive rights to all future film soundtracks from the filmmaker, according to The Hollywood Reporter India.

The first two months of 2026 added two more prestige investments. In January, Jio Studios picked up a 50.1 per cent stake in Sikhya Entertainment — the production house behind Masaan and The Lunchbox — for approximately ₹150 crore. In February, Universal Music Group acquired a 30 per cent stake in Excel Entertainment, the banner co-founded by Ritesh Sidhwani and Farhan Akhtar, at an enterprise valuation of ₹2,400 crore.

"It's an era of acquisitions and consolidation. Either major studios will fold into larger structures, or new forms of non-traditional financing will define the next phase."

— Independent producer, speaking to THR India

Why the Money Stopped — and Started Again

Industry insiders trace the consolidation wave to a funding vacuum that formed after 2022. When global streamers entered India around 2015–16, they injected aggressive capital, pushing up budgets and star fees. Spending peaked during the pandemic as platforms acquired content at inflated prices to sustain subscriber growth.

"But then, the crazy money stopped. Suddenly, studios were staring at liquidity gaps," a senior production house executive told THR India. "Industrial financing has practically disappeared over the last five to ten years."

By the time streamer budgets normalised, theatrical revenues had not fully recovered and traditional financiers had largely exited. Studios that once patched budgets film-by-film found themselves needing structural capital. The result, according to analysts, was a tilt toward equity deals that offer stable cash flows rather than the volatility of single theatrical releases.

Bollywood films lost a four-percentage-point share at the box office in 2024, dropping to 40 per cent from the previous year, according to an Ormax Media report. Yet Hindi films grossed ₹5,504 crore in 2025, with tentpole releases like Dhurandhar (over ₹1,000 crore) and Chhaava (over ₹800 crore) carrying the bulk of collections, according to Livemint.

South Expansion and New Producers

The consolidation drive has coincided with a southward expansion. Bollywood production houses, multiplex chains, and even actor-producer Ajay Devgn are forging partnerships in South India, where moviegoing frequency runs 2 to 2.2 times higher than in Hindi-speaking markets, according to Bhuvanesh Mendiratta, managing director of Miraj Entertainment.

"Investing in the south today is a very logical business call," Mendiratta told Livemint, citing consistent audience turnout, strong VFX infrastructure in Hyderabad, and the reliable commercial performance of southern stars.

At the same time, more than a dozen new production houses have sprung up across Mumbai since 2022. B62 Studios, founded by Uri: The Surgical Strike director Aditya Dhar, has already delivered its fourth production venture. Civic Studios, incubated at MIT Media Lab, is building a global content pipeline. Bhanushali Productions, founded by a former T-Series executive, has produced at least six films.

"Most of the new production companies aim to make content-led, story-driven films that do not necessarily need huge budgets," Karan Taurani, senior vice president at Elara Securities, told Livemint.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, the restructuring carries direct implications. Studios are increasingly viewing international markets and festival circuits as core revenue streams rather than afterthoughts. Excel's deal with Universal Music Group includes global distribution rights for all future soundtracks. Directors like Zoya Akhtar, Vikramaditya Motwane, and Bhansali are developing content for Netflix and Amazon Prime Video, platforms available in 190 and 240 countries respectively. Civic Studios has offices in both Mumbai and London.

The global push means diaspora audiences can expect a wider and more consistent pipeline of Indian-origin content, from arthouse films premiering at Cannes and TIFF to franchise tentpoles reaching screens in North America and Europe.

Risks and the Road Ahead

Not everyone is sanguine. A filmmaker who has worked under both independent and corporate-backed models warned THR India that consolidation could narrow creative output. "If too much money sits with too few entities, one dominant kind of cinema may emerge," the filmmaker cautioned.

Others argue the opposite. If cash flow is secure, deep-pocketed backers could fund riskier, more original films alongside profitable franchise titles. The tension between spreadsheet logic and creative instinct will define how the new studio system evolves.

About 85 Hindi films released theatrically in 2024, and only around 10 collected meaningful box office revenue, according to Livemint. Whether corporate capital can fix those odds — or simply raise the stakes — is the question Bollywood's next act will have to answer.
